summary:
San Luis Potosí stands under the national framework of Mexico, where legal gender recognition remains unevenly implemented. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date, and set out a per-state compliance picture showing that implementation differs sharply from one state to another. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

San Luis Potosí is among the states that have acted. The state began authorising legal gender changes for transgender people on 17 May 2019, following a 2019 reform of the Civil Registry Law that created an administrative recognition procedure with implementing regulations issued by gubernatorial decree. The state is listed among the states that enacted a gender-identity law in 2019.

Partnership recognition is settled here as well. Same-sex marriage took effect in San Luis Potosí on 21 May 2019, after the state Congress voted 14-12 in favour on 16 May 2019, and joint adoption by same-sex couples has been legal in the state from the same month. Nationally, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.

The state's hate-crime statutes recognise motivation by gender and sexual preference, which gives trans victims a route to aggravated treatment of an attack. Its local anti-discrimination law bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender but does not name gender identity, leaving a gap in the statutory protection a trans visitor would be able to invoke.

The distance between statute and practice is the recurring national finding. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions explicitly that the work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Violence against trans people is documented at national scale. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many states operate administrative recognition procedures while calling on those that lack them to adopt them. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police, and set those barriers against killings, including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, killings that drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

Two official responses frame what a trans visitor can expect from authorities. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide, a statute named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished and which activists describe as critical to their sense of safety. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

No region-specific incident, enforcement or ordinance evidence was found for San Luis Potosí, and no border-screening or document-procedure information specific to the state is recorded.
tangentialFactors:
San Luis Potosí's 2019 measures place it in the larger group of Mexican states that legislated recognition and marriage reform in that year, rather than marking it as an outlier. The national picture at March 2025 was 22 of 32 states with a recognition procedure, so a trans traveller crossing state lines moves between materially different document regimes, and the Human Rights Watch backgrounder of 31 March 2025 is the source that sets out the per-state compliance picture.

The state's protection machinery is partial in a way that matters for comparison. Hate-crime statutes here recognise gender and sexual preference as motivations, while the anti-discrimination law omits gender identity; other states name gender identity expressly, and Mexico City has gone further by criminalising transfemicide through the Paola Buenrostro law of July 2024.

Enforcement is the variable that national comparisons keep returning to. Beer's LSE USAPP analysis of 22 November 2024 finds progressive legislation rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights warned in 2024 that impunity for LGBTI violations may have reached alarming levels while demanding that investigations respect gender identity.

Violence indicators give scale to that gap: Transgender Europe records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021 and 52 in the year to September 2023, behind Brazil's 100, with at least three transgender people killed in the opening weeks of 2024 including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, and Agencia Presentes reporting a rise in attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders over the twelve months to June 2024.

outOfScopeNotes:
No incident, enforcement outcome or ordinance specific to San Luis Potosí was found in the sources reviewed, so the state's practical record on recognition requests, hate-crime prosecutions and police handling of trans complaints remains unresolved and not sourced here.

The Human Rights Watch backgrounder of 31 March 2025 is described as setting out a per-state compliance picture, but the specific compliance entry for San Luis Potosí is not reproduced in the sources reviewed; whether the state's 2019 procedure operates without obstruction is unresolved.

No border-screening, port-of-entry document inspection or visa-procedure information specific to San Luis Potosí or to Mexico is recorded, and nothing in the sources indicates how federal immigration screening treats a passport whose gender marker conflicts with presentation.

The gap between the anti-discrimination law's omission of gender identity and the hate-crime statute's recognition of gender motivation is stated in the sources without explanation of how the two are applied together in practice; case-level application is not sourced.
